explanations.explanation: Peace, friend! Paul says that since we have been justified through faith, "…we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ…" Notice he says "we have," not "we might get some someday." It's already in the box.

I get why debt came to mind, because plenty of people feel like they owe somebody. But Paul doesn't say we have debt with God. He says that since we have been justified through faith, "…we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ…"

Distance isn't what Paul says, friend. He says that since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God. Right after that he says we have "…gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." So the word Paul uses here is peace.

I know, the working-hard idea is a comfy one, because most of life runs on it. But Paul says the opposite. He says Jesus is the One "…through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." The access comes by faith, not by effort.
Right, friend, it's False. Paul says we have gained access "…by faith into this grace in which we stand." He never says we got in by working hard enough. That access comes through Jesus.
Hope is the word, baker. Paul says, "And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." That comes right after he says we stand in this grace, so we're not rejoicing from shaky ground.
Fear is a sneaky one, because plenty of us carry it around. But Paul doesn't say we rejoice in fear. He says we rejoice "…in the hope of the glory of God." Fear never shows up in that verse.
A shadow sounds poetic, I'll give you that. Paul doesn't use it here, though. He says, "And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." The word he picked is hope.

Yes, our sufferings. Paul says, "Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings…" I know, I did a double take too. He doesn't say suffering feels good. He says we rejoice in it because of what we know it produces.

That would be an easier verse to read, wouldn't it? But Paul doesn't say we rejoice in our good deeds. He says, "…we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance…" That's his reason, and it keeps going: perseverance, then character, then hope.

Rejoicing in our own strength is what I'd expect from a guy flexing in the mirror. Paul says something else. He says, "…we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance…" No strength talk here, baker.
Perseverance is it. Paul says, "…we know that suffering produces perseverance…" That's the reason he gives for rejoicing. It's the first link in his chain.
Bitterness is what I'd guess on my worst day, I'll admit it. But Paul doesn't say suffering produces bitterness. He says it produces perseverance, and that's where the chain starts.
Weakness feels like the natural answer, baker. Paul says something else, though. He says, "…we know that suffering produces perseverance…" Perseverance is the word in that verse.
True! Paul says, "…perseverance, character; and character, hope." So the chain runs from suffering to perseverance to character to hope. And hope is where he lands.
Close, but it's True. Paul says, "…perseverance, character; and character, hope." So the last link is hope, and character is what produces it. That's the end of the chain.

explanations.answer: God has poured out His love into our hearts
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says, "…hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts…" The hope rests on God's love, and Paul says that love has already been poured out into our hearts.

explanations.answer: We have earned it by enduring our hardships
explanations.explanation: Enduring does show up in the chain, but it's not the reason Paul gives here. He says hope does not disappoint us "…because God has poured out His love into our hearts…" The reason is God's love, not our earning.

explanations.answer: God has taken all suffering out of our lives
explanations.explanation: That one sounds nice, but Paul says the opposite just before this. He says, "…we also rejoice in our sufferings…" So suffering is still in the picture. The reason hope doesn't disappoint is that "…God has poured out His love into our hearts…"

The Holy Spirit, yes! Paul says God has poured out His love into our hearts "…through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us." So the Spirit is a gift God has given. That's a lot of good packed into one verse.
His prophets is a fair guess, but it's not what Paul says here. He says God poured out His love into our hearts "…through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us." The Holy Spirit is the answer.

Angels are impressive, and the angel who called me out of that drawer still makes me a little nervous. But Paul doesn't say angels here. He says God poured out His love into our hearts "…through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us."
The ungodly, baker. Paul says, "…while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly." Christ didn't wait for us to get strong first. He died for us while we were powerless.
That would make a tidy sentence, wouldn't it? But Paul says, "…while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly." The word is ungodly, not faithful.
Worthy is a nice thought, but it's not what Paul says. He says, "…while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly." He never says he died for the worthy.
Paul says the opposite, baker. He says, "Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man…" So he calls it very rare, not common. Then he says someone might possibly dare to die for a good man.

It's False, baker. Paul says, "Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die." Very rarely is not common. That sets up how much bigger verse 8 is.

explanations.answer: Christ died for us while we were still sinners
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, "But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." The proof came while we were still sinners. We weren't cleaned up first, and Christ died for us anyway.

explanations.answer: Christ died for us after we turned our lives around
explanations.explanation: That's the other order, baker. Paul says, "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." So it's not after we turned our lives around. It was while we were still sinners.

explanations.answer: Christ blessed us after we proved ourselves faithful
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a rewards program, which I respect. But Paul says, "…God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." The proof is Christ's death for us while we were still sinners, not our faithfulness.

True, baker. Paul says, "Therefore, since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him!" I think Paul is excited here, and I would be too. We've been justified by His blood, and we'll be saved from wrath through Him.

It's actually True. Paul says, "…since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him!" So the text says we'll be saved from wrath through Him. Justified by His blood now, saved from wrath through Him.

The death of His Son, baker. Paul says, "…if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son…" Reconciled means brought back together. He did that for us when we were enemies.

Offerings at the temple is a fair guess, but Paul doesn't name them here. He says, "…when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son…" The reconciling comes through the Son's death.
I've made plenty of those promises, like swearing off a third cookie at midnight. But Paul doesn't say we were reconciled that way. He says, "…we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son…"
Life, baker. Paul says, "…how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!" We were reconciled through His death, and saved through His life. Paul is stacking it up.
His words matter a lot in the Gospels, but that's not what Paul says here. He says, "…how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!" The word is life.
Miracles is a fair guess, but Paul doesn't say miracles here. He says, "…how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!" The word he uses is life.
God Himself, baker. Paul says, "…we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation." We rejoice in God, and it all comes through Jesus.
The apostles is a fair guess, but that's not what Paul says. He says, "…we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ…" The rejoicing is in God.

Angels are impressive, no argument from me. But Paul doesn't say we rejoice in the angels. He says, "…we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation."
